name: Reminders That Work, and Reminders That Do Not
title: Reminders That Work, and Reminders That Do Not
answer: This idea is that reminders to students work when they come from someone the student knows, such as their own counselor, and when they name the student's actual next step. It matters because large campaigns that send generic messages at scale have often failed to change aid or enrollment, while counselor-sent messages have helped some students take college steps. AI can help counselors send personal reminders at a scale they could not manage by hand, but the relationship remains the active ingredient.

sections.body: The idea addresses a common mistake in college and career support: assuming that more messages, sent to more students, will produce more action. The text reports that several large trials show the source of a reminder matters, and that a national campaign sending similar messages from an outside organization had mostly no effect. Students tend to respond to people they know, so a reminder from a counselor can carry weight that a generic message does not. The problem is not a lack of information alone, but a lack of connection and specificity. AI can help a counselor personalize reminders at scale, but it does not replace the counselor's relationship with the student.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, a counselor can draft messages about upcoming deadlines and use the school's texting platform to send them to the right students, naming the student's actual next step, such as submitting a transcript or finishing a financial aid form. The counselor's name and a way to reply make the message personal. Deadline tracking tools help counselors and students stay organized, and platforms such as Scoir and BigFuture let students track their applications and deadlines. A counselor can see which students are behind and reach out, with the tool keeping the list and the counselor keeping the relationship. The text does not give grade bands for this practice, so it applies to the counseling, college, and career setting it describes.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text reports several large trials on reminders, and in Texas, text messages from students' own counselors raised college steps and enrollment for some groups of students (Avery et al., 2021). A national campaign that sent similar messages from an outside organization had mostly no effect. Two trials of national and state financial aid campaigns involved about 800,000 students and found no effect on aid or enrollment (Bird et al., 2021). A national trial with 785,000 students tested brochures, emails, texts, and application fee waivers to encourage enrollment at selective colleges, and it also found no change (Gurantz et al., 2020). The text concludes that scale alone does not produce results and that messages must reach students through a relationship and address their specific situation.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are clear in the text: reminders from an outside organization had mostly no effect, and large financial aid and enrollment campaigns found no change even when they reached hundreds of thousands of students. Size by itself does not create results, so sending more messages is not a substitute for a relationship or for addressing a student's specific situation. The decisions that stay with a person include what next step to name, which students to contact, and how to reply when a student responds. The counselor keeps the relationship, while the tool keeps the list. AI can help draft and send personal reminders at scale, but it does not replace the counselor's judgment or connection with the student.
